bib.title: Natural Language Processing with Python, Chapter 6: Learning to Classify Text
bib.venue: O'Reilly Media (book chapter; year inferred from the O'Reilly NLTK book, not printed in the chapter text)

question: How can features of language data be identified and used to build supervised classifiers (decision trees, naive Bayes, maximum entropy) for NLP tasks, and how should they be evaluated?
contributions: Walks through supervised classification with NLTK on gender identification, document classification, POS tagging, sentence segmentation, dialogue acts and RTE
Explains train / dev-test / test splitting and error analysis, plus accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure, confusion matrices and cross-validation
Explains decision trees (entropy, information gain), naive Bayes (smoothing, independence assumption) and maximum entropy classifiers (generative vs conditional)

results.claim: Naive Bayes with only the last letter as feature classifies name gender at 75.8% on a 500-name test set.
results.setup: NLTK Names Corpus (male + female names, shuffled), featuresets[500:] train, featuresets[:500] test, NaiveBayesClassifier, feature = last_letter
results.note: Single random shuffle, no seed; the exact numbers vary run to run.

results.claim: A kitchen-sink feature set (first/last letter, letter counts, letter presence) overfits and scores about 1 point lower than the last-letter feature.
results.setup: Names Corpus, same 500-name test split, NaiveBayesClassifier, gender_features2 (firstletter, lastletter, count(x), has(x) for 26 letters)
results.note: The text says accuracy is 'about 1% lower'.

results.claim: With the last-letter feature, accuracy on the 1,000-name dev-test set is 76.5%.
results.setup: Names Corpus split: train_names=names[1500:], devtest_names=names[500:1500], test_names=names[:500]; NaiveBayesClassifier; last_letter feature
results.note: Train set size is not stated in the chapter; Exercise 2 implies 6,900 train, 500 dev-test, 500 test, which does not match the code split (1,000 dev-test).

results.claim: Adding two-letter suffix features raises dev-test accuracy from 76.5% to 78.2% after error analysis.
results.setup: Names Corpus dev-test set (names[500:1500]), NaiveBayesClassifier, features suffix1 and suffix2
results.quote: improves by almost three percentage points (from 76.5% to 78.2%)
results.note: The text says 'almost three percentage points' but 78.2 - 76.5 = 1.7 points; the paper's wording is inconsistent with its own numbers.

results.claim: Naive Bayes on bag-of-words presence features over the 2,000 most frequent words reaches 81% accuracy on 100 held-out movie reviews.
results.setup: NLTK Movie Reviews Corpus (pos/neg), documents shuffled, featuresets[100:] train, featuresets[:100] test, NaiveBayesClassifier, binary contains(word) features over 2,000 most frequent lowercased words
results.note: Test set is only 100 documents (the chapter's own lower bound for a meaningful test). Total corpus size is not stated. all_words.keys()[:2000] relies on Python 2 FreqDist ordering by frequency.

results.claim: In the movie review classifier, the word 'outstanding' is the most informative feature (pos:neg 11.1:1) and 'seagal' signals negative at 7.7:1.
results.setup: Same naive Bayes movie review classifier, show_most_informative_features(5)
results.note: Other top features: seagal 7.7 neg, wonderfully 6.8 pos, damon 5.9 pos, wasted 5.8 neg.

results.claim: Most informative name-gender feature is last letter 'a' (female:male 38.3:1) and 'k' (male:female 31.4:1).
results.setup: Naive Bayes name gender classifier with last_letter feature, show_most_informative_features(5)

results.claim: A decision tree POS tagger using only common-suffix features (100 most common 1-3 character suffixes) reaches 62.7% accuracy.
results.setup: Brown corpus, news category tagged words, 10% test / 90% train split taken by position (no shuffle), DecisionTreeClassifier, features endswith(suffix) for 100 most common suffixes
results.note: Test set size in words is not printed.

results.claim: Adding the previous word as a feature (plus suffixes 1-3) lifts naive Bayes POS accuracy to 78.9%.
results.setup: Brown news tagged sentences, per-word featuresets, first 10% test / rest train, NaiveBayesClassifier, features suffix(1..3) and prev-word
results.note: Baseline is a different classifier (decision tree) with different features, so the gain mixes the classifier and the feature change.

results.claim: A consecutive (greedy sequence) tagger that also uses the previously predicted tag reaches 79.8% accuracy.
results.setup: Brown news tagged sentences, size = 10% of sentences held out as test, ConsecutivePosTagger with NaiveBayesClassifier, features suffix(1..3), prev-word, prev-tag
results.note: Split is by sentence here and by word in Example 6-4, so the two are not exactly comparable.

results.claim: Treating sentence segmentation as period/question/exclamation classification with naive Bayes gives 97.4% accuracy.
results.setup: treebank_raw sentences merged into a token list; featureset per token in '.?!' with next-word-capitalized, prevword, punct, prev-word-is-one-char; first 10% test, rest train; NaiveBayesClassifier
results.note: Test size not printed. No majority-class baseline is given.

results.claim: Naive Bayes bag-of-words dialogue act classifier over 15 act types scores 66% on NPS Chat.
results.setup: NPS Chat Corpus, first 10,000 posts, 15 dialogue act labels, binary contains(word) features from nltk.word_tokenize lowercased, first 10% test / 90% train, NaiveBayesClassifier
results.note: Test size is 1,000 posts by arithmetic (10% of 10,000); the chapter does not print it.

results.claim: A shallow word-overlap RTE classifier (nltk.classify.rte_classify) reaches just over 58% on the combined RTE test data.
results.setup: RTE Challenge data; features word_overlap, word_hyp_extra, ne_overlap, ne_hyp_extra after stopword removal; classifier type and dataset sizes not stated
results.quote: reaches just over 58% accuracy on the combined RTE test data
results.note: Binary True/False task, so chance is near 50%.

results.claim: Confusion matrix of the Section 5.4 unigram tagger on Brown editorial: NN for JJ errors affect 1.6% of words and NN for NNS 1.5%.
results.setup: Unigram tagger t2 from Section 5.4 evaluated on brown.tagged_sents(categories='editorial'); ConfusionMatrix(gold, test); row = reference, col = test
results.quote: substitution of NN for JJ (for 1.6% of words), and of NN for NNS (for 1.5% of words)
results.note: Largest diagonal cell: NN 11.8% of words.

results.claim: The 95% accuracy of an always-majority word-sense classifier shows why accuracy depends on label frequency.
results.setup: Hypothetical word sense of 'bank': financial sense in 19 of 20 occurrences of financial newswire versus a balanced corpus where the most frequent sense is 40%
results.quote: an accuracy of 95% would hardly be impressive

results.claim: Rule of thumb: 100 evaluation instances suffice for few, balanced labels; otherwise make the rarest label appear at least 50 times; with plenty of data use 10% for evaluation.
results.setup: General guidance on test set sizing, no experiment
results.quote: the size of the test set should be chosen to ensure that the least frequent label occurs at least 50 times
results.note: Also: 'can be performed with as few as 100 evaluation instances' and 'using 10% of the overall data for evaluation'.

results.claim: A hidden Markov model must avoid scoring all tag sequences: a 30-tag set gives about 600 trillion labelings of a 10-word sentence.
results.quote: there are about 600 trillion (3010) ways to label a 10-word sentence
results.note: '3010' in the text is 30^10 with lost superscript.

results.claim: Expected Likelihood Estimation smoothing adds 0.5 to each count(f, label).
results.setup: Naive Bayes P(f|label) estimation; NLTK nltk.probability offers other smoothing methods
results.quote: basically adds 0.5 to each count(f,label) value

results.claim: No head-to-head accuracy comparison of naive Bayes versus maximum entropy (or decision tree) is reported in the chapter; it is left as Exercise 5.
results.setup: Whole chapter: every measured accuracy uses NaiveBayesClassifier except the POS decision tree (62.7%); maxent is only described
results.quote: build three classifiers for the task: a decision tree, a naive Bayes classifier, and a Maximum Entropy classifier
results.note: Exercise 5 text. The qualitative claim is that a conditional model can beat a generative one on questions 1 and 2 because it has fewer free parameters.

limits: Every accuracy is a single run on one random shuffle or positional split with no seed, no repeated runs and no confidence interval; the movie review test set is 100 documents.
Only name gender and POS have tested feature variants; naive Bayes is used almost everywhere, and maximum entropy is never trained or scored in the chapter (exercise only).
Sentence segmentation and dialogue act results have no majority-class baseline, so 97.4% and 66% cannot be judged against chance.
The chapter glosses over the mathematics (points to Section 6.9 further reading) and says the pure-Python NLTK learners are too slow for large datasets.

Dated: Python 2 code (print statements, FreqDist.keys() sorted by frequency, suffix_fdist.inc, zip returning a list, nltk.TaggerI usage); the book predates scikit-learn, logistic regression with regularisation, embeddings and transformers; all numbers are 2009-era NLTK results.

Example 6-6 as printed is buggy: 'for i, word in words' needs enumerate, classifier.classify(words, i) does not match the featureset interface, and the function never returns sents. Example 6-1 has an en dash in name[–1].
Chapter says 'four RTE Challenges' to date; RTE accuracy of 58% is on a task where chance is about 50%.
practices: Split labeled data into training, dev-test and test sets; use dev-test for error analysis and keep the test set unused until development ends (p.225, p.256 summary).
Change the dev-test/training split each time error analysis is repeated, so the classifier does not reflect idiosyncrasies of the dev-test set (p.227).
Start with a kitchen-sink feature set and prune by checking which features help, but beware overfitting on small training sets (p.224-225).
Use nltk.classify.apply_features to avoid holding all featuresets in memory on large corpora (p.224).
Build the test set from different documents, or better different genres, than the training set, rather than random sentence shuffling within one genre (p.238-239).
Choose test set size so the rarest label occurs at least 50 times; use about 10% of data when data is plentiful (p.238).
Read accuracy against label frequencies; use precision, recall and F-measure for search-style tasks with many irrelevant items (p.239-240).
Use a confusion matrix when there are three or more labels to see which confusions dominate (p.240-241).
Use cross-validation with N folds when annotated data is scarce, and check the variance across folds (p.241).
Prune decision trees or stop splitting when the training data in a node becomes small (p.245).
Use smoothing (for example Expected Likelihood Estimation) for naive Bayes so unseen feature/label pairs do not zero out a label (p.249).
Avoid highly correlated features in naive Bayes because they are double counted (p.250).
Train maximum entropy models with Conjugate Gradient or BFGS rather than GIS or IIS, which are considerably slower (p.251).
Use a generative model only when questions 3-6 are needed; a conditional model may do better on label prediction alone (p.254).
For large datasets, use NLTK's interfaces to external learners (Weka, Mallet, TADM, MegaM) instead of the pure-Python classifiers (p.237, p.256).

terms.definition: the task of choosing the correct class label for a given input
a classifier built from training corpora containing the correct label for each input
a dictionary mapping feature names to simple-typed values (Booleans, numbers, strings)
the part of the development set held out from training, used for error analysis
relying on idiosyncrasies of the training data that do not generalize, especially with too many features and small training sets
the ratio between label frequencies for a feature value, such as female:male = 38.3:1 for names ending in a
find the most likely label for the first input, then use that answer to help label the next input
the percentage of inputs in the test set that the classifier correctly labeled
TP/(TP+FP)
TP/(TP+FN)
the harmonic mean of precision and recall, (2 x Precision x Recall)/(Precision+Recall)
a table where each cell [i,j] indicates how often label j was predicted when the correct label was i
subdivide the corpus into N folds, train on all but one fold, test on that fold, and combine the scores
a decision tree with a single node that decides how to classify inputs based on a single feature
H = -sum over labels of P(l) x log2 P(l); high when labels are varied, low when one label dominates
the original entropy of the labels minus the weighted average entropy of the stump's leaves
every feature is independent of every other feature given the label
techniques for estimating P(f|label) that avoid zero probabilities for unseen feature/label pairs
each combination of labels and features that receives its own parameter in a Maximum Entropy model
a classifier that models the joint probability P(input, label), as naive Bayes does
a classifier that models P(label|input), as Maximum Entropy does
descriptive models capture patterns in the data; explanatory models postulate the causal relationships behind them
